under s. 7 in Thomson Newspapers, supra, because these records are
"created" in response to state compulsion, and do not arise from the
ordinary (private) course of business, merely to be "located" by the
individual.  With respect, I do not agree.  In my view,
hail reports and
fishing logs should be seen to constitute the "ordinary" records of
those licensed to participate in the groundfish fishery; the fact that these
records are statutorily required, and would not exist but for s. 61 of the Act,
does not suddenly turn them into compelled testimony of the kind that is taken
during an investigation into wrongdoing
.
Hail reports and fishing logs
are required from all commercial fishers and assist in the routine
administration of the Fisheries Act, quite apart from any investigation into
wrongdoing
.
They are produced by all the participants in the regulatory
sphere, not just by one person in response to a criminal investigation
;
they are therefore similar to the pre-existing business records considered in
Thomson Newspapers.

[298]

In applying the relevant legal principles,
the defendant’s contention that the prosecutor had acted improperly by adducing
evidence or commenting on the defendants refusal to cooperate or speak
respectively with the ESA Inspector and ESA Investigator is not necessarily
improper nor does it infringe the defendant’s right to silence.  This is
because the defendant’s charges are strict liability regulatory offences being
tried in a non-jury situation and in which the
Electricity Act, 1998
,
does statutorily require an individual in certain circumstances to cooperate
and provide documents or things to an ESA inspector.  Accordingly,  evidence on
the defendant’s refusal to speak or corporate with the ESA inspector or ESA investigator
is relevant and can be admitted in respect to evidence on the defendant’s due
diligence used to avoid committing the offences, or as relevant evidence in
respect to the defendant’s credibility, or on the issue of recent fabrication
where a claim that someone else did the electrical work is later adduced by the
defendant as a defence.  On the other hand, evidence of the defendant’s refusal
to cooperate or refusal to answer questions from the ESA Inspector and ESA
Investigator would not be evidence that can be used to prove guilt.

[299]

Again,
as the admissibility and consideration
of the evidence of the defendant’s lack of cooperation and refusal to answer
questions from the ESA inspector and ESA investigator is an evidentiary issue,
the
defendant’s concern about the prejudicial effect of such evidence is lessened
because this is a non-jury trial and the charges involved strict liability
regulatory offences, in which the trier would be mindful of applying the
relevant legal principles and law and any evidence that contravenes the right
to silence can be disabused and given no weight, and that such evidence would
not be used as proof of any of the elements of the offence, nor would it be
used improperly as proof of guilt.

[300]

Therefore, the prosecutor’s conduct in
regards to leading relevant evidence on the defendant’s failure to cooperate
with ESA Inspector Shaun Smith and the defendant’s refusal to speak with ESA
Investigator Gary Corbett would not be inappropriate, and as such the
prosecutorial conduct has not caused an unfair trial, nor prejudiced the integrity
of the judicial process, which would be
manifested, perpetuated or
aggravated through the conduct of the trial, or by its outcome.

(xii)
The
prosecutor had argued with the defendant directly rather than speaking or
making
submissions
through the court

[301]

The defendant also contends that the
prosecutor had acted improperly when he had argued directly with the defendant
when the defendant had been testifying, instead of making submissions through
the court.  The defendant submits that this had occurred when the prosecutor
had been complaining about the defendant’s convoluted testimony and whether the
defendant would call any witnesses to corroborate the defendant’s testimony,
when the prosecutor then opined that at the end of the day the defendant was
going to say that it was a conspiracy.  Then when the defendant replied to the
prosecutor, “No, that’s your opinion though”, the defendant contends that the
prosecutor had addressed the defendant directly while the defendant was still
testifying in-chief, by the prosecutor stating to the defendant that the
prosecutor believed that is what the defendant was going to say, that it was a conspiracy
against the defendant and that everyone is lying.  However, the defendant then responded
to the prosecution’s suggestion by informing the court that to the prosecutor,
the defendant was already guilty, but that the defendant had been proving that
the prosecutor was not right and that what the prosecutor was saying is not
correct or true.

[302]

Furthermore, on the issue
of potential witnesses that the defendant could call, the defendant also contends
that the prosecutor had directly stated to the defendant that the prosecutor would
be delighted, tickled, and elated to see and hear these people, and to get an
opportunity to cross examine these people.

[303]

In response to the
defendant’s contention that the prosecutor had improperly argued directly with
the defendant when he had been testifying, the prosecution submits that the
defendant had been both simultaneously a witness and his own advocate, so that
arguing directly with the defendant when the defendant was testifying would
have been when the defendant had been speaking in his role as his own advocate
and not as a witness.

[304]

Although the prosecutor
may not have been following proper decorum and traditional principles of advocacy
when arguing with the defendant directly about whether the defendant was going
to call any witnesses to corroborate the defendants’ testimony about what
others had supposedly told him, or what other people had supposedly done when
the defendant was testifying, those supposed arguments from the prosecutor could
have also been questions to test the defendant’s credibility or simply
procedural questions on whether those witnesses with that evidence or
information would be called to corroborate the defendant’s claims.

[305]

Furthermore,
as this particular
contention also concerns evidentiary issues,
the defendant’s concern
about the prejudicial effect of the prosecutor arguing with the defendant directly
while in the witness stand is lessened because this is a non-jury trial and the
charges involve strict liability regulatory offences, for which the trier would
be mindful of applying the relevant legal principles and law and any
prejudicial effect from the prosecutor arguing directly with the defendant while
the defendant was testifying can be disabused and not be considered negatively
or as proof of any of the elements of the offence, nor would it be used
improperly as proof of guilt.

[306]

Therefore, the prosecutor’s conduct in arguing directly with the
defendant while the defendant had been testifying would not have prejudiced the
fairness of the trial, nor prejudiced the integrity of the judicial process,
that would be manifested, perpetuated or aggravated through the conduct of the
trial, or by its outcome.

(xiii)
The
prosecutor had threatened to request the maximum penalty available for the
defendant for arbitrary reasons

[307]

Moreover, the defendant contends that
the prosecutor had acted improperly when the prosecutor had threatened to seek
the maximum penalty if the defendant were convicted of committing the three
offences.

[308]

In response, the prosecution submits that the defendant’s contextualization
of the prosecutor’s comments about seeking the maximum penalty is incorrect, as
the prosecution contends that the prosecutor had merely wanted to ensure that
the defendant had every opportunity to call the witnesses he required so that the
defendant could make full answer and defence and have a fair trial, since the
prosecutor would be seeking the maximum penalty available under the
Electricity
Act, 1998
, if the defendant were convicted.  Moreover, the prosecution submits
that the prosecutor had made that comment in the course of offering to consent
to an adjournment, so that the defendant could secure witnesses that the defendant
had wished to call and that the defendant would have sufficient time to bring
those witnesses to court, even if further trial dates were needed, because the
prosecutor would be seeking the maximum penalty under the statute if the defendant
was found guilty.

[309]

In respect to the prosecutor’s comment at issue, it is ambiguous
what the prosecutor meant when he stated, “I would suggest that you even give
this individual – and he didn’t even ask for it, maybe we didn’t hear him, but
time to get these people.  Get summonses out to make full representation, full
defence, full.  Because I am very curious because if in fact you do find him
guilty, I’m gonna be asking for maximum penalty.  I don’t know what he done to
these witnesses – to the victims, but also in terms of what he’s done in terms
of the Court’s time.”

[310]

However, in any context, the prosecutor making a comment that he
would be seeking the maximum penalty before the defendant had even been
convicted would not be a harmless comment and would be undermine the
prosecutor’s role as a quasi-minister of justice.  And, it would have been more
harmful if this had been a jury trial, as it gives the potential impression
that the defendant has committed the most serious of offences, considering that
the prosecutor had been seeking the maximum penalty before the evidentiary
portion of the trial had even been completed.

[311]

But since this is not a jury trial, the trier who heard and
perceived the impugned comments and in the context when the comments would have
been made, would be able to consider their effects on the defendant, their
prejudice to the fairness of the trial and on the outcome of the trial, as well
as its prejudice to the integrity of the judicial process.  In this particular
situation, the prosecutor’s comment about seeking the maximum penalty if the
defendant were convicted did not cause the defendant to receive an unfair
trial, nor did it undermine the integrity of the judicial process, since the
trier would be cognizant of applying the relevant legal principles and law and
would also be able to disabuse and give no weight to the prosecutor’s comment,
nor to use negatively or improperly as proof of guilt.

[312]

Hence, the prosecutor’s conduct in making an inappropriate
submission about seeking the maximum penalty is not prosecutorial conduct that
had caused an unfair trial, nor had it prejudiced the integrity of the judicial
process, that would be manifested, perpetuated or aggravated through the
conduct of the trial, or by its outcome.

(8)
The
Main Category: Did The Prosecutor’s Conduct During The Trial Prevent The
Defendant From Having A Fair Trial?

[313]

To reiterate, the defendant contends
that as a result of the cumulative effect of the prosecutor’s improper conduct,
which consisted of many indiscretions during the trial when the defendant was
unrepresented, the defendant maintains that he had been unable to receive a
fair trial, and as such, there is a basis for finding an abuse of process under
the main category.

[314]

However, much of the defendant’s grounds
for a claim of abuse of process concerned evidentiary issues that involved the
prosecutor adducing or eliciting prejudicial evidence from leading questions to
his own witnesses, prejudicial hearsay evidence, prejudicial bad character
evidence, prejudicial opinion evidence, and irrelevant prejudicial evidence.
In addition, the defendant also contends that
the prosecutor’s sarcastic
comments, insults, mocking language, and demeaning tone has also prejudiced the
defendant’s right to a fair trial.

[315]

After applying the relevant legal principles in respect to these evidentiary
issues raised by the defendant, the prosecutor had not adduced evidence
inappropriately, as the evidence in question were for the most part relevant to
issues in this case.  Moreover, the defendant’s concern about the prejudicial
effect of evidence that had been adduced from leading questions put by the
prosecutor to their own witnesses and the elicitation of irrelevant hearsay,
bad character, and lay opinion evidence into the trial, has to be viewed in
context and its intended use in the trial, but any prejudicial effect of the
impugned evidence had been lessened as this was a non-jury trial and the
charges involved strict liability regulatory offences in which the prosecution
can elicit evidence in their case-in-chief to rebut a defence of due diligence
or other anticipated defences.

[316]

And, in respect to the claim that the prosecutor’s sarcastic
comments, insults, mocking language, and demeaning tone has caused the
defendant prejudice and an unfair trial, the trier who heard and perceived the
impugned comments, and in the context when the comments would have been made,
would be able to consider their effects on the defendant, their prejudice to
the fairness of the trial and on the outcome of the trial.

[317]

Ergo, after considering the impugned evidentiary issues and the
context in which the prosecutor’s impugned comments, language, and tone were
used and what had been occurring in the trial at the time, the cumulative
effect of the prosecutor’s conduct, although not ideal and of perfect
comportment, did not go beyond aggressive to abusive so as to cause the
defendant to receive an unfair trial, since the defendant’s trial was a
non-jury trial for which the trier would be cognizant of applying the relevant
legal principles and law, and would also be able to disabuse and give no weight
to any hearsay, bad character, opinion, or any other irrelevant prejudicial
evidence, nor put any weight on any inappropriate, sarcastic, or demeaning
comments made by the prosecutor about the defendant’s memory, business
practices, or personal lifestyle, or to improperly use the impugned evidence or
the immoderate comments of the prosecutor as proof of guilt.

[318]

Accordingly, the defendant’s right to a fair trial has not been
prejudiced by the cumulative effect of the prosecutor’s conduct in eliciting
the impugned evidence, nor by the prosecutor’s impugned comments, language or
tone, that would be manifested, perpetuated or aggravated through the conduct of
the trial, or by its outcome.

(9)
The
Residual Category: Did The Prosecutor’s Conduct During The Trial Cause
Prejudice To The Integrity Of The Judicial Process?

[319]

For this branch of the test for abuse
of process, the defendant also contends that the cumulative effect of the
prosecutor’s improper conduct during the trial when the defendant was
unrepresented also undermined the integrity of the judicial process.

[320]

However, to reiterate, Moldaver
J.
emphasized,
at paras.
35 and 44
,
in
R. v. Babos
,
2014 SCC 16 (CanLII)
, [2014] S.C.J. No. 16
(S.C.C.),
that finding abuse of process under the
residual category is indeed exceptional and very rare and that when the
residual category is invoked, the question is whether the state has engaged in
conduct that is offensive to societal notions which underlie the community’s
sense of fair play and decency and whether proceeding with a trial in the face
of that conduct would be harmful to the integrity of the justice system.  In
addition, Moldaver noted that at times, state conduct would be so troublesome
that having a trial, even a fair one, would leave the impression that the
justice system condones conduct that offends society's sense of fair play and
decency  [
emphasis is mine below
]:

By
contrast,
when the residual category is invoked, the question is whether the
state has engaged in conduct that is offensive to societal notions of fair play
and decency and whether proceeding with a trial in the face of that conduct
would be harmful to the integrity of the justice system
. To put it in
simpler terms, there are limits on the type of conduct society will tolerate in
the prosecution of offences.
At times, state conduct will be so troublesome
that having a trial - even a fair one - will leave the impression that the
justice system condones conduct that offends society's sense of fair play and
decency
. This harms the integrity of the justice system.
In these kinds
of cases, the first stage of the test is met
.

…

Undoubtedly,
the balancing of societal interests that must take place and the "clearest
of cases" threshold presents an accused who seeks a stay under the
residual category with an onerous burden.
Indeed, in the residual category,
cases warranting a stay of proceedings will be "exceptional" and
"very rare"
(
Tobiass
, at para.
91
). But this is as it should be.
It is only where the "affront to fair play and decency is disproportionate
to the societal interest in the effective prosecution of criminal cases"
that a stay of proceedings will be warranted (
R. v. Conway
,
1989 CanLII 66 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R.
1659
, at p. 1667)
.

[321]

And, to recap, much of the defendant’s
bases for a claim of abuse of process concerned evidentiary issues involving
the prosecutor adducing or eliciting evidence from the use of leading questions
to his own witnesses and from hearsay, bad character, lay opinion, and
irrelevant evidence, which the defendant contends is prosecutorial conduct that
has contravened notions of fundamental justice, and therefore, undermines the
integrity of the judicial process.  In addition, the defendant also contends
that
the prosecutor’s sarcastic comments, insults, mocking language,
and demeaning tone towards the defendant during the trial is, as well, prosecutorial
conduct that has further
undermined the integrity of
the judicial process.

[322]

After applying the relevant legal principles and after taking
into consideration the impugned evidentiary issues and the context in which the
prosecutor’s impugned comments, language, and tone were used and what had been
occurring in the trial at the time, the cumulative effect of the prosecutor’s
conduct, although not ideal and of perfect comportment, did not go beyond
aggressive to abusive so as to
contravene notions of
fundamental justice, which would offend society's sense of fair play and
decency.  Ergo, the prosecutor’s conduct did not undermine the integrity of the
judicial process
, since the defendant’s trial was a non-jury trial for
which the trier would be cognizant of applying the relevant legal principles
and law and would also be able to disabuse and give no weight to any hearsay,
bad character, opinion, or any other irrelevant prejudicial evidence, nor put
any weight on any inappropriate, sarcastic, or demeaning comments made by the
prosecutor about the defendant’s memory, business practices, or personal
lifestyle, or to improperly use the impugned evidence or the prosecutor’s
intemperate comments as proof of guilt.

[323]

Consequently, the cumulative effect of the prosecutor’s conduct
has not reached a degree of unfairness or vexatiousness that contravenes
notions of fundamental justice, nor is it the type of conduct in which the
justice system would find it necessary to intervene so that it would not leave
the impression that it condones conduct that offends society's sense of fair
play and decency.  Therefore, the prosecutor’s conduct during the trial has not
undermined the integrity of the justice system that would be manifested,
perpetuated or aggravated through the conduct of the trial, or by its outcome.

(10)
Disposition
Of The Abuse Of Process Application

[324]

As a result, the defendant has failed
to establish on a balance of probabilities that the cumulative effect of the prosecutor’s
conduct had made the trial unfair or that it has undermined the integrity of
the judicial process,
that would be manifested, perpetuated or aggravated
through the conduct of the trial, or by its outcome.

[325]

Accordingly, the defendant’s
application for a finding of an abuse of process and a remedy is dismissed.

In
J.
Anthony Van Duzer’s
textbook, “
The Law of Partnerships and Corporations, 2nd. ed.
” (Toronto,
Canada: Irwin Law Inc., 2003), the author summarizes the legal status of a
general partnership on pp. 86 to 88, and emphasizes that a partnership has no legal
existence separate from the partners who make it up, and that the individual
partners have an unlimited personal liability for the obligations of the
partnership business, and that all partners are liable for all obligations
incurred in the course of the partnership business while they are partners [
emphasis
is mine below
]:

A partnership has no
existence separate from the partners who make it up
. A number of
significant consequences flow from this fact, the most important of which are
that
partners have unlimited personal liability for the obligations of the
partnership business
and, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary,
partnerships may be dissolved by any of the partners.
Partnerships come
into existence without any formality; it is sufficient if two or more persons
begin to carry on business together with a view to a profit.
In each case,

the existence of a partnership will be determined by whether the parties
intended to enter into such a relationship
. The
fundamental test for such
an intention is whether the business is being carried on for the benefit of the
alleged partners
.  The most significant indicia of such an intention is
sharing profits from the business activity, though one must be careful to
distinguish other relationships in which profits are shared, such as some
creditor/debtor and co-ownership relationships.
Other important indicia
include participation in the management and control of the partnership and
common ownership of property. No single factor is conclusive. Whether a
partnership exists depends on the circumstances of each case
.

The relationship of
partners to each other is governed by default rules in partnership legislation
that operate unless the parties agree on some other arrangement. The
relationship between partners and third parties dealing with the partnership is
governed by a set of mandatory rules.
In general, all partners are liable
for all obligations incurred in the course of the partnership business while
they are partners
. After a person dies or becomes bankrupt, he will not be
liable for obligations incurred afterwards. If he leaves the partnership in
other circumstances, he may continue to be liable for new obligations of the
partnership unless he was never known to be a partner by the person to whom the
partnership owes the obligation, or notice is given that he has ceased to be a
partner.
Persons who are not partners will nevertheless be liable as
partners if they knowingly allow themselves to be held out as partners
.

Partnership agreements
are a critical complement to the law of partnerships. The default provisions of
partnership legislation governing the relations among partners provide an
inadequate and out-of-date skeleton of a structure not suitable for most
partnerships. Often the default rules governing the relations among partners,
including those dealing with management, interests in profits and capital,
membership in the partnership, and dissolution, will need to be changed. It
will also be desirable, in most circumstances, to create monitoring and control
arrangements for the purpose of reducing the likelihood of unauthorized
behaviour by partners, procedures to govern how the partnership is to act
collectively, and provisions to deal with how liability imposed under
partnership law will be allocated among the partners.

Finally, we looked at
contractual joint ventures and limited partnerships. Joint ventures, although
they are not partnerships, may have some lesser partnership-like legal
consequences. In some circumstances, joint venturers owe each other a fiduciary
duty not to put their personal interests ahead of the interests of the venture
and have liability for obligations incurred in connection with the venture.
Limited partnerships are like general partnerships except that the liability of
at least one partner is limited to the amount she invested in the partnership.
Such limited partners also have restrictions on their ability to participate in
management. If a limited partner violates the restrictions, he loses his
limited liability and becomes a general partner.

had asked the defendant for his WSIB number and liability insurance information,
the defendant had provided a specific WSIB number and an insurance policy
number for Gore Mutual Insurance (see Exhibit 6).

[376]

Furthermore, the defendant during his testimony had
indicated that he had a partner when he had provided the WSIB number and
insurance policy number to Ahmed Khan.  The defendant then testified that his
partner was someone named Ali Nabbouh and then provided a telephone number for
that individual.  ESA Investigator Gary Corbett then called Nabbouh’s telephone
number on the morning of February 2, 2017, when the defendant was testifying and
left a message on the Nabbouh’s voice mail system.  Nabbouh then returned ESA
Investigator Corbett’s call later that morning and informed Corbett that he was
not partners with the defendant.  Nabbouh then appeared in the courthouse later
that day on February 2, 2017, and when the defendant tried to speak to Nabbouh
outside the courtroom, Nabbouh did not wish to speak with the defendant.
Nabbouh then entered the courtroom and testified as a witness for the defence.
During his testimony, Nabbouh testified that he was not in partnership with the
defendant, that he did not recognize the WSIB number nor the insurance policy
number in Exhibit 7, and then said that he had already told that to ESA
Investigator Corbett.  Furthermore, Nabbouh did confirm that he had met with
the defendant once, but that they did not agree to be partners in any venture.
In addition, Nabbouh also stated that he would not have given his WSIB number
or insurance policy number to anyone he had just met and who he did not know.

a)
Did the
prosecution have to disclose the conversation between Ali Nabbouh and ESA
Investigator to the defendant prior to Ali Nabbouh testifying, even though the
defendant was the party calling Ali Nabbouh?

[377]

A critical issued has arisen in respect to Ali
Nabbouh’s testimony as a defence witness.  It arose during Ali Nabbouh’s
testimony when Nabbouh had testified that he was not in partnership with the
defendant and then clearly stated that he had already told that to ESA
Investigator Corbett.  However, ESA Investigator Corbett had only spoken to
Corbett just that morning when Nabbouh had returned Corbett’s voice mail.
Therefore, the Nabbouh conversation with the ESA investigator had not been
disclosed to the defendant, nor was the court informed about a conversation
that had taken place between Nabbouh and the ESA Investigator that had just occurred
a few hours before Nabbouh had arrived in court to testify.  The existence of
that conversation between Nabbouh and the ESA investigator only came to light
because Nabbouh had testified that he already told ESA Investigator Gary
Corbett earlier in their telephone conversation that Nabbouh had not been in
partnership with the defendant.

[378]

Ergo, based on Ali Nabbouh’s testimony, the issue
is whether the prosecution in failing to disclose Ali Nabbouh’s conversation
with ESA Investigator Corbett that had occurred earlier in the morning of February
2, 2017, had infringed the defendant’s right to disclosure under
s. 7
of the

Charter
.  The prosecution had an obligation to disclose the contents of that
conversation to the defendant, as part of the prosecution’s ongoing obligation
to disclose all relevant evidence that comes into the prosecution’s possession.
More importantly, the prosecution had a legal obligation to disclose the
contents of Nabbouh’s conversation with the ESA investigator, even though it
was the defendant who would be calling Ali Nabbouh to testify for the defence
about their intended partnership and about the veracity of the WSIB number and
the liability insurance policy number that Ali Nabbouh supposedly gave to the
defendant, which was then provided to Ahmed Khan, the homeowner of 291 Boon
Avenue, Toronto.  Thus, the prosecution has failed to comply with their ongoing
obligation to disclose that relevant evidence to the defendant.  Moreover, if
the prosecution had not failed to disclose Nabbouh’s conversation with the ESA investigator,
then the defendant may not have called Ali Nabbouh as a defence witness,
considering that if the defendant had known what Nabbouh had communicated to
ESA Investigator Corbett that there had been no partnership between Nabbouh and
the defendant, as well as knowing that Ali Nabbouh had been upset about being
brought into the defendant’s trial, then the defendant would have been in an
informed position to decide whether or not to call Ali Nabbouh as a defence
witness.

[379]

On the other hand, once the defendant testified
that the WSIB number and insurance policy number had belong to his partner, who
the defendant had mentioned was a person named Ali Nabbouh, then Nabbouh’s
testimony on whether Nabbouh had been in a partnership with the defendant, as
well as the veracity of the WSIB number and liability insurance policy number
would have been relevant to supporting and establishing a partnership between
Nabbouh and the defendant.  Thus, even if the defendant would have decided not
to call Nabbouh if he had been informed about the contents of Nabbouh’s
conversation with the ESA Investigator, the prosecution, in any event, likely
would have called Nabbouh as a rebuttal witness to rebut the defendant’s
testimony about having a partner on the 291 Boon Avenue, Toronto renovation,
after the defendant had completed presenting his defence.

[380]

In
R. v. Bjelland
,
2009 SCC 38 (CanLII)
, [2009] S.C.J. No. 38, at
paras.17 to  27, the Supreme Court held that before a party is entitled to a
remedy under
s. 24(1)
, the party seeking such a remedy must establish a breach
of his or her
Charter
rights.  Moreover, the Supreme Court held that the
Crown's failure to disclose evidence does not, in and of itself, constitute a
violation of
s. 7
; rather, an accused must generally show "actual
prejudice to their ability to make full answer and defence”, in order to be
entitled to a remedy under
s. 24(1)
.  Also, the Supreme Court noted that the
appropriate focus in most cases of late or insufficient disclosure under
s.
24(1)
is the remediation of prejudice to the accused, as well as safeguarding
the integrity of the justice system would be a relevant concern.  The Supreme
Court also held that the exclusion of evidence may be warranted where the
evidence is produced mid-trial after important and irrevocable decisions about
the defence have been made by the accused.  And, for purposes of trial fairness,
the Supreme Court also explained that only where prejudice cannot be remedied
by an adjournment and a disclosure order would exclusion of evidence be an
appropriate and just remedy.  However, the Court also recognized that there may
also be instances where an adjournment and disclosure order may not be
appropriate because admission of evidence compromises the integrity of the
justice system.  Furthermore, in clear cases, the Supreme Court held that the
exclusion of evidence may be an appropriate and just remedy under
s. 24(1)
in
order to preserve the integrity of the justice system [
emphasis is mine
below
]:

The remedy of exclusion of evidence will normally
arise under
s. 24(2)
of the
Charter
. Section 24(2) applies to evidence obtained
in a manner that infringes or denies a person the rights or freedoms granted by
the Charter. But such evidence will only be excluded if its admission would
bring the administration of justice into disrepute. Section 24(2) provides:

Where, in proceedings under subsection 1, a court concludes that
evidence was obtained in a manner that infringed or denied any rights or
freedoms guaranteed by this
Charter
, the evidence shall be excluded if it is
established that, having regard to all the circumstances, the admission of it in
the proceedings would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

Remedies under
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter
are flexible
and contextual
:
Doucet-Boudreau v. Nova Scotia (Minister of Education),
2003 SCC 62
,
[2003] 3
S.C.R. 3
, at paras.
41
, 52 and 54-56. They address the most varied situations.
Different considerations may come into play in the search for a proper balance
between competing interests.
Section 24(1)
provides:

Anyone whose rights or freedoms, as guaranteed by this
Charter
, have
been infringed or denied may apply to a court of competent jurisdiction to
obtain such remedy as the court considers appropriate and just in the
circumstances.

Here, we are concerned with aspects of the conduct of
a criminal trial and of the operation of the justice system, where the courts
have to pass upon the guilt or innocence of an accused.
While the exclusion
of evidence will normally be a remedy under s. 24(2), it cannot be ruled out as
a remedy under
s. 24(1)
.
However,
such a remedy will only be available in
those cases where a less intrusive remedy cannot be fashioned to safeguard the
fairness of the trial process and the integrity of the justice system
.

Before being entitled to a remedy under
s. 24(1)
, the
party seeking such a remedy must establish a breach of his or her
Charter

rights
. In a case
of late disclosure, the underlying Charter infringement will normally be to
s.
7
.
Section 7
of the Charter protects the right of the accused to make full
answer and defence. In order to make full answer and defence,
the Crown must
provide the accused with complete and timely disclosure
:
see
R. v.
Stinchcombe
,
1991 CanLII 45 (SCC)
,
[1991] 3 S.C.R. 326
. The purpose underlying the Crown's obligation
to disclose is explained by Rosenberg J.A.
in R. v. Horan,
2008 ONCA 589
,
237
C.C.C. (3d) 514
, at para.
26
:

Put simply, disclosure is a means to an end.
Full prosecution
disclosure is to ensure that the accused receives a fair trial, that the
accused has an adequate opportunity to respond to the prosecution case and that
in the result the verdict is a reliable one
.

However, the Crown's failure to disclose evidence does
not, in and of itself, constitute a violation of
s. 7
.
Rather,
an accused must generally show
"actual prejudice to [his or her] ability to make full answer and defence
"
(
R. v. O'Connor
,
1995 CanLII 51 (SCC)
,
[1995] 4 S.C.R. 411
, at para.
74
)
in order to be entitled
to a remedy under
s. 24(1)
.

While the accused must receive a fair trial, the trial
must be fair from both the perspective of the accused and of society more
broadly
.
In
R. v.
Harrer
,
1995 CanLII 70 (SCC)
,
[1995] 3 S.C.R. 562
, McLachlin J. (as she then was) provided guidance
on what is meant by trial fairness. She stated, at para. 45, that:

At base,
a fair trial is a trial that appears fair, both from the
perspective of the accused and the perspective of the community. A fair trial
must not be confused with the most advantageous trial possible from the
accused's point of view
:
R. v. Lyons
,
1987 CanLII 25 (SCC)
,
[1987] 2 S.C.R. 309
, at p. 362,
per
La Forest J. Nor must it be conflated with the perfect trial; in the real world,
perfection is seldom attained.
A fair trial is one which satisfies the
public interest in getting at the truth, while preserving basic procedural
fairness for the accused
. [Emphasis added.]

Apart from ensuring trial fairness, there is one other
circumstances in which late disclosed evidence might be excluded. That is where
to admit the evidence would compromise the integrity of the justice system.

Thus, a trial judge should only exclude evidence for
late disclosure in exceptional cases: (a) where the late disclosure renders the
trial process unfair and this unfairness cannot be remedied through an
adjournment and disclosure order or (b) where exclusion is necessary to
maintain the integrity of the justice system. Because the exclusion of evidence
impacts on trial fairness from society's perspective insofar as it impairs the
truth-seeking function of trials, where a trial judge can fashion an
appropriate remedy for late disclosure that does not deny procedural fairness
to the accused and where admission of the evidence does not otherwise
compromise the integrity of the justice system, it will not be appropriate and
just to exclude evidence under
s. 24(1)
.

This view is reflected
in
cases such as
O'Connor

that have considered whether a stay is the appropriate remedy for late or
insufficient disclosure under
s. 24(1)
. As L'Heureux-Dubé J., for the
majority,
stated in
O'Connor
, at para.
83
:

In such circumstances [of late or
insufficient Crown disclosure and
a consequent
s. 7
breach], the court must fashion a just and appropriate
remedy, pursuant to
s. 24(1)
.
Although the remedy for such a violation will
typically be a disclosure order and adjournment,
there may be some extreme
cases where the prejudice to the accused's ability to make full answer and
defence or to the integrity of the justice system is irremediable
.
In
those "clearest of cases", a stay of proceedings will be appropriate.

This statement recognized that
the appropriate
focus in most cases of late or insufficient disclosure under
s. 24(1)
is the
remediation of prejudice to the accused, but that safeguarding of the integrity
of the justice system will also be a relevant concern
. Of course
the
prejudice complained of must be material and not trivial.
For example, the
exclusion
of evidence may be warranted where the evidence is produced mid-trial after
important and irrevocable decisions about the defence have been made by the
accused
. Even then,
it is for the accused to demonstrate how the late
disclosed evidence would have affected the decisions that were made. For
purposes of trial fairness, only where prejudice cannot be remedied by an
adjournment and disclosure order will exclusion of evidence be an appropriate
and just remedy
.

There may also be instances where an adjournment and
disclosure order may not be appropriate because admission of evidence
compromises the integrity of the justice system
. For example, as Rosenberg J.A.
stated in

Horan
, at para.
31
:

In some cases, an adjournment may not be an appropriate or just remedy
if the result would be to unreasonably delay the trial of an in-custody
accused. In such a case, an appropriate remedy could be exclusion of the
undisclosed evidence. However, the burden is on the accused to demonstrate that
exclusion of the evidence was appropriate.

In other words, where an accused is in pre-trial
custody, an adjournment that significantly prolongs the custody before trial
may be seen as compromising the integrity of the justice system.
The
exclusion of evidence may also be an appropriate and just remedy where the
Crown has withheld evidence through deliberate misconduct amounting to an abuse
of process
.
Yet even in such circumstances, society's interest in a fair
trial that reaches a reliable determination of the accused's guilt or innocence
based on all of the available evidence cannot be ignored
. This will
especially be true where the underlying offense is a serious one:
see
O'Connor
,
at para.
78
.
In clear cases, however, the exclusion of evidence may be an
appropriate and just remedy under
s. 24(1)
in order to preserve the integrity
of the justice system
.

[381]

As the defendant’s right to disclosure would
have applied to Ali Nabbouh’s conversation with ESA Investigator Corbett, then the
prosecution should have disclosed to the defendant the evidence of Nabbouh’s
conversation with the ESA Investigator that had occurred in the morning of February
2, 2017, just hours before Nabbouh appeared in court to testify and prior to
the court hearing Nabbouh’s testimony.  However, there is no evidence that this
omission by the prosecutor had been intentional or deliberate, considering that
Ali Nabbouh was intended to be called as a defence witness and the conversation
had only occurred very shortly before Nabbouh actually testified.  On the other
hand, the defendant did not know what Nabbouh would be intending to say in his
testimony, even though it was the defendant who had wanted to call Nabbouh as a
defence witness to support the defendant’s claim about having a partner in the
291 Boon Avenue, Toronto renovation and that the WSIB number and liability
insurance policy number had been provided to the defendant from his partner.  In
contrast, ESA Investigator Gary Corbett would have had an inkling what Ali
Nabbouh would be saying in his testimony in light of their conversation on the
telephone earlier that morning.  Furthermore, even though Ali Nabbouh had been treated
as a witness for the defendant, the conversation that Nabbouh had with the ESA
investigator had not been disclosed to the defendant as would have been
required by the prosecution, as part of the prosecution’s ongoing obligation to
disclose all relevant evidence that comes into the prosecution’s possession.  Then
again, even though there is no evidence that the prosecutor had been made aware
of what Ali Nabbouh would be saying in his testimony, or that the ESA investigator
had indeed informed the prosecutor about the contents of that conversation between
Nabbouh and the ESA investigator, there would have been enough time after the
conversation between Nabbouh and the ESA Investigator had taken place for ESA Investigator
Corbett to inform the prosecutor what the contents of that conversation had
been.

[382]

Ergo, if the contents of the conversation
between Nabbouh and ESA Investigator Corbett would have been disclosed to the
defendant prior to Nabbouh testifying, then the defendant may have chosen not
to have Ali Nabbouh testify on behalf of the defence, as the defendant would
have also likely realized that Nabbouh was potentially not a witness that would
be favourable to the defendant.

[383]

And, because Ali Nabbouh’s conversation with the
ESA Investigator had not been disclosed to the defendant, nor was the court
informed about a conversation that had taken place between Nabbouh and the ESA
Investigator just a few hours before Nabbouh arrived in court to testify, the
omission or failure to disclose this conversation had prejudiced the
defendant’s right to make full answer and defence.  More importantly, if the
defendant would have been made aware of the contents of that conversation
between Nabbouh and the ESA Investigator, the defendant may have chosen not to
call Nabbouh or if the defendant had still wished to call Nabbouh as his
witness, the defendant would have at least realized that Nabbouh would probably
not be a witness favourable to his defence.  In which case, if the defendant
opted to not call Nabbouh as his witness, then the prosecutor would have had to
wait until the defendant had finished presenting his defence before the prosecution
could call Ali Nabbouh as a rebuttal witness, and after the prosecutor would
have disclosed to the defendant a will-say for what Nabbouh’s testimony would
entail.

[384]

Moreover, because this omission by the
prosecution to disclose the contents of the conversation between Ali Nabbouh
and ESA Investigator Corbett to the defendant has prejudiced the defendant’s
ability to make full answer and defence, then
s. 7
has been infringed and since
the remedy of an adjournment and costs would not remedy the prejudice, then excluding
Ali Nabbouh’s testimony would be the appropriate remedy under
s. 24(1)
to
remedy the prejudice to the defendant’s right to make full answer and defence.
Accordingly, Ali Nabbouh’s testimony will be excluded and disabused and carry
no weight in these proceedings.

that Jairam also did some work for her employer.  Bacchus also said that her
place of employment is only a few doors away from Jay Jairam’s autobody

observe the defendant actually doing any of the electrical work on her house

electrical work associated with the pot lights and associated switches and

contact the ESA about the defendant and that it had been the ESA who had
approached Bacchus first.  Moreover, the defendant had commenced or done work

[407]

Accordingly, the defendant’s suggestion that the

(b)
Conclusion On Whether The
Prosecution Has Proven Beyond A Reasonable Doubt The Defendant Has Committed
The Actus Reus Of The Offence For The Three Charges

[451]

The defendant testified that he did not do any of
the electrical work in any of the three houses in question.  In a case where an
accused testifies in a trial, then the test established by the Supreme Court in

R. v. W. (
D.
)
,
1994 CanLII 76 (SCC)
, [1994] S.C.J. No. 91 (S.C.C.) applies.  Cory J. in
R.
v. W. (
D.
)
, at para. 23, summarized three scenarios for acquitting the
accused: First of all, if the trier-of-fact believes the evidence of the
accused then there must be an acquittal. Next, if the testimony of the accused
is not believed, but the trier-of-fact is still left with reasonable doubt by
that testimony, then the trier-of-fact must acquit.  And finally, even if the
testimony of the accused does not create reasonable doubt, the trier-of-fact
must still be convinced on the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the
accused is guilty of committing the offence:

First, if
you believe the evidence of the accused, obviously you must acquit.

Second, if you do not believe the
testimony of the accused but you are left in reasonable doubt by it, you must
acquit.

Third, even if you are not left in doubt by the
evidence of the accused, you must ask yourself whether, on the basis of the
evidence which you do accept, you are convinced beyond a reasonable doubt by
that evidence of the guilt of the accused.

[452]

With respect the defendant’s testimony that he
did not do any of the electrical work in any of the three houses does not
create reasonable doubt or have any validity for the houses at 22 Vespahills
Crescent, Brampton or 291 Boon Avenue, Toronto.  Both respective homeowners of
those two houses, Jay Jairam and Ahmed Khan, had testified to personally seeing
the defendant doing electrical work in their respective houses; that the
defendant had told them both that he had was an electrician; and that
electrical permits had not been taken out for the electrical work at those two
houses.  For the third house at 94 Narrow Valley Crescent, Brampton, the homeowner,
Razeka Bacchus, did not observe the defendant doing any electrical work in her
house, nor is there evidence that an electrical permit had not been taken out
for 94 Narrow Valley Crescent, Brampton.

[453]

In addition, even if all three homeowners were
aware and knew that the defendant was not a licenced electrician or a licenced
electrical contractor, or that they had special arrangements or business
relationships to make money together on other endeavours and the homeowners had
still agreed to having the defendant do the electrical work for their
respective renovations, the defendant was still not legally permitted to do any
electrical work covered by the
Ontario
Electrical Safety Code
, O. Reg.
164/99, on their three houses without being a licensed electrician or licenced
electrical contractor in Ontario.  In other words, the three homeowners could
not give permission to the defendant to do any electrical work on their three
houses, which would exempt the defendant from the application of s. 3 of the
Licensing
Of Electrical Contractors And Master Electricians
Regulation (
Electricity
Act, 1998
),
O. Reg. 570/05
.

[454]

Furthermore, when the electrical work that had
been done at the two houses located 22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton and 291
Boon Avenue, Toronto, in regards to the defendant’s renovation work of those
two houses, had been inspected by the ESA, both inspections uncovered defects
or errors in the electrical work that a licenced electrician probably would not
have done.  In addition, Sean Smith testified that a licenced electrical
contractor or licenced electrician would have taken out a permit for the
electrical work at  22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton.  Moreover, when Jay Jairam
had asked the defendant about the electrical permit for the electrical work
being done at 22 Vespahills Crescent, the defendant scolded Jairam for not
trusting him and that Jairam would get a Certificate of Inspection from the ESA
at the end.  Moreover, no electrical permits had been taken out for the
electrical work at 22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton and 291 Boon Avenue,
Toronto, for which the ESA inspectors had inspected the electric work that had
been done at those houses as part of the renovation work.

[455]

For Razeka Bacchus’s house at 94 Narrow Valley
Crescent, Brampton,  there is no evidence that the ESA inspectors had inspected
the electric work that had been done in the renovation of Bacchus’s house or
whether anyone searched for the existence of an electric permit being taken out
for the house at 94 Narrow Valley Crescent, Brampton, during the relevant time.

[456]

Therefore, the electrical work that had been
done at the two houses located at 22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton and 291 Boon
Avenue, Toronto, were likely done by an unlicenced person.  The defendant is
such a person.  In addition, there is no credible evidence that a licenced
electrician or licenced electrical contractor had done any of  the electrical
work at those houses when the defendant was doing the renovation of those two
houses.  Accordingly, the defendant’s testimony that he did not do any of the
electrical work at 22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton and 291 Boon Avenue,
Toronto is not plausible or credible.

[457]

However, for the Razeka Bacchus’s house at 94 Narrow
Valley Crescent, Brampton, Bacchus did not specifically testify that the
defendant would be doing the electrical work in her renovation, nor did she
actually see the defendant doing any electrical work in her house.  Bacchus
also said she had understood that the defendant would be doing all the
renovation work, but that if the defendant did not know how to do something
then the defendant would bring in someone who had the proper licence to do it.
Accordingly, the prosecution has not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the
defendant had done the electrical work at 94 Narrow Valley Crescent, Brampton
or that he had been “operating an electrical contracting business
without holding a valid electrical contractor licence” in
respect to the electrical work done at 94 Narrow Valley Crescent, Brampton.

[458]

In sum, the prosecution has only proven that the
defendant has committed the
actus reus
beyond a reasonable doubt for the
offences set out in count #1, in respect to the house at 22 Vespahills
Crescent, Brampton and for count #2 in respect to the house at 291 Boon Avenue,
Toronto, but has failed to prove the defendant has committed the
actus reus

of the offence for the charge set out in count #3 in respect to the house at 94
Narrow Valley Crescent, Brampton.  As such, an acquittal will be entered for
the defendant on count #3.  Therefore, the defendant will only have to prove
the defence of due diligence on a balance of probabilities for counts #1 and
#2, if the defendant does not wish to be convicted of committing the offences
set out in counts #1 and #2.

(3)
Due Diligence Defence

(a)
Did The
Defendant Establish The Defence Of Due Diligence In Respect To Each Of The
Charges On A Balance Of Probabilities

[459]

Even though the prosecution has proven the defendant has
committed the
actus reus
of the offence set out in s. 3 of the
Licensing
Of Electrical Contractors And Master Electricians
Regulation (
Electricity
Act, 1998
),
O. Reg. 570/05
beyond a reasonable doubt in respect to counts
#1 and #2, the defendant is still entitled to an acquittal in a prosecution of
a strict liability offence, if the defendant can prove he has a defence of due
diligence on a balance of probabilities by showing that he had taken all
reasonable steps for the circumstances to avoid the particular event or to
prove that they had reasonably believed in a mistaken set of facts, if true,
would render his act or omission innocent:
R. v. Sault Ste. Marie
(1978),

1978 CanLII 11 (SCC)
, 40 C.C.C. (2d) 353 (S.C.C.).

[460]

In short, the defendant has the onus to prove he had not been
negligent in “operating an electrical contracting business without holding a
valid electrical contractor licence”, contrary to s. 3 of the
Licensing Of
Electrical Contractors And Master Electricians
Regulation (
Electricity Act,
1998
),
O. Reg. 570/05
.  Moreover, the defendant will be found guilty of
committing this offence if he is unable to prove on a balance of probabilities
either branch of the due diligence defence established in
R. v. Sault Ste.
Marie
, of taking all reasonable care for the circumstances to not operate
an electrical contracting business without holding a valid electrical
contractor licence or that he had operated as an electrical contractor without
holding an electrical contractor’s licence because he had reasonably believed that
he had not been required to obtain an electrical contractor licence.

[461]

For his due diligence defence, the
defendant submits that he did not know that Steve Duff was not a licenced electrician
in respect to 291 Boon Avenue, Toronto and that the defendant had used the
defendant’s electrician at 22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton, but cannot recall
the electrician’s name.

[462]

Although the prosecution has proven
that the defendant has committed the
actus

reus
of the offence
for count #1 and count #2, the defendant can still be acquitted if he meets his
legal and evidential burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that he
had taken all reasonable care to avoid committing the offence or he had been
operating under a mistaken set of facts which if true would make his act or
omission innocent.

(i)
count #1: 22 Vespahills
Crescent, Brampton

[463]

In respect to the electrical work that
had been done at 22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton, there is no evidence that a
properly licenced electrician or licenced electrical contractor in Ontario had
done any of the electrical work at 22 Vespahills Crescent.  Even if the
defendant had not been the person who did the electrical at 22 Vespahills
Crescent and that some other person had indeed done the electrical work, there
is no evidence of who that other person is or that this other person had been a
licensed electrician or licenced electrical contractor in Ontario.

[464]

In respect to the two branches of the
due diligence defence, there is no evidence that the defendant had taken all
reasonable care to avoid not doing any electrical work at 22 Vespahills
Crescent or that the defendant had been under a reasonable belief or a set of
mistaken set of facts that he could legally do electrical work  at 22
Vespahills Crescent without holding a valid electrical contractor licence.

[465]

As a consequence, the defendant has not
met its burden in proving on a balance of probabilities that the defendant had
taken all reasonable care in the circumstances to avoiding committing the
offence of
“operating an electrical contracting business without holding
a valid electrical contractor licence”
or that the
defendant had been under a reasonable mistake of fact, if true, would make the
act innocent.  Accordingly, the defendant is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt of
committing the offence set out in count #1.

(ii)
Count #2: 291 Boon Avenue,
Toronto

[466]

For the electrical work that had been
done at 291 Boon Avenue, Toronto, there is no evidence that a properly licenced
electrician or licenced electrical contractor in Ontario had done any of the
electrical work at the 291 Boon Avenue house.

[467]

The prosecution has proven beyond a reasonable
doubt that the electrical work done at 291 Boon Avenue had been first done at
the beginning by the defendant and then later in December of 2013, when the
defendant fell behind and obtained authorization from Ahmed Khan and had
brought in Steve Duff to help the defendant do the electrical work.  After Steve
Duff had been brought in by the defendant, Ahmed Khan had also observed both
the defendant and Steve Duff doing the electrical work together.  It had been
only after Ahmed Khan lost contact with the defendant that Ahmed Khan had hired
Steve Duff’s company Wiztronic Inc. separately to fix the electrical work in
the basement done by the defendant and to complete the electrical work for the
whole house.  However, the prosecution has proven beyond a reasonable doubt
that Steve Duff had not been a licenced electrician or licenced electrical
contractor in Ontario.

[468]

In his defence, the defendant said he
did not know that Steve Duff had not been a licensed electrician, but that
would not apply to the time before the defendant had brought Duff in to help
the defendant, when the defendant had been actually observed by the homeowner,
Ahmed Khan, doing electrical work at 291 Boon Avenue.  In particular, Ahmed
Khan, the homeowner  of 291 Boon Avenue, had already observed the defendant
doing electrical work in the basement before Khan had given the defendant
permission to bring in Steve Duff to help the defendant with the electrical
work.  As such, the defendant’s claim that he did not know Steve Duff was not
properly licenced would not be relevant to the electrical work that the
defendant had previously done in the basement of 291 Boon Avenue, and would
only be relevant to the electrical work that both the defendant and Steve Duff
had done together at 291 Boon Avenue when the defendant was still responsible
for the electrical work.  Furthermore, the defendant’s claim of not having any
knowledge of Steve Duff not being properly licenced as an electrician does not
apply to the electrical work that had been done by Steve Duff after Ahmed Khan
had hired Wiztronic Inc. separately and independent of the defendant to fix the
electrical work already done in the basement by the defendant and to complete
the electrical work for the rest of the house.

[469]

Furthermore, when the defendant had
brought in Steve Duff to help him do the electrical work at 291 Boon Avenue in
Toronto, there is no evidence that the defendant had taken the appropriate
steps or effort to verify with the appropriate governing body that Steve Duff
was a qualified electrician or a licensed electrical contractor in Ontario.  As
the person ultimately responsible for the renovation work at 291 Boon Avenue,
Toronto because of the written agreement he had with the homeowner Ahmed Khan,
the defendant had an obligation to the homeowner to ensure that the electrical
work was being done properly and according to the
Ontario
Electrical Safety
Code
, O. Reg. 164/99, by a qualified and licensed electrician in Ontario.
Therefore, the defendant should have taken steps to verify Steve Duff’s
qualifications to do electrical work and because there is no evidence that he
did take any steps to verify Steve Duff’s qualifications as a licenced
electrician or licenced electrical contractor in Ontario, then the defendant’s
belief that Steve Duff was a licenced electrician or licenced electrical
contractor in Ontario is not a reasonable mistake of fact which would make the
defendant’s act or omission innocent.

[470]

In addition, since the defendant could not take out an electrical
permit from the ESA because the defendant was not licenced as an electrician or
an electrical contractor in Ontario, then it would have been logical for the
defendant to have Steve Duff obtain the electrical permit from the ESA in
Duff’s name for 291 Boon Avenue, if the defendant had truly believed that Duff
was a licenced electrician.  There is no evidence that the defendant had asked
Duff to apply for an electrical permit for 291 Boon Avenue.

As well, to protect the defendant from any
liability for any electrical work that Steve Duff would have done in the 291
Boon Avenue house, considering that the defendant had agreed to be responsible
for the renovation of 291 Boon Avenue, then it would have also been logical for
the defendant to ask Duff if he had been properly licenced as an electrician or
an electrical contractor in Ontario or to ask Duff for his electrical
contractor’s licence number issued by the ESA.  Therefore, the defendant cannot
reasonably claim as a mistake of fact that he did not know that Steve Duff was
not properly licenced, when there is no evidence that he had made reasonable
inquiries into whether Steve Duff had been properly licenced as an electrician
or an electrical contractor in Ontario.

[471]

Therefore, in respect to the two
branches of the due diligence defence, there is no evidence that the defendant
had taken all reasonable care to avoid not doing any electrical work at 291
Boon Avenue or that the defendant had been under a reasonable belief or a set
of mistaken set of facts that he could legally do electrical work at 291 Boon
Avenue without having a valid electrical contractor licence.

[472]

As a consequence, the defendant has not
met its burden in proving on a balance of probabilities that the defendant had
taken all reasonable care in the circumstances to avoiding committing the
offence of
“operating an electrical contracting business without holding
a valid electrical contractor licence”
or that the
defendant had been under a reasonable mistake of fact, if true, would make the
act innocent.  Accordingly, the defendant is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt of
committing the offence set out in count #2.

(iii)
count #3: 94 Narrow Valley
Crescent, Brampton

[473]

Since the prosecution has not proven
beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant had committed the
actus reus

of the offence of
“operating an electrical contracting business without
holding a valid electrical contractor licence”
in
regards to the house at 94 Narrow Valley Crescent, Brampton, then defendant is
not required to establish the defence of due diligence for count #3, and the
defendant will be acquitted of committing the charge set out in count #3.

(4)
Did The Prosecution Prove Beyond A Reasonable
Doubt That The Defendant Had Been Operating An Electrical Contracting Business Without
Holding A Valid Electrical Contractor Licence For All Three Houses?

[474]

In respect to count #1, the defendant, who was not a licensed
electrician or a licenced electrical contractor in Ontario, had informed Jay
Jairam, the homeowner of 22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton that he was an
electrician.  Jairam had hired the defendant to renovate his basement,
including doing the electrical work.  The defendant had worked on the
renovation of Jairam’s house from April 1, 2014 to July 22, 2014.  Jairam also
said that no electrical work had been previously done in the basement of
Jairam’s house and that no licenced electrical contractor had been hired
previously to do any electrical work in the basement.  Jairam also testified to
having observed the defendant running and pulling wire in the basement, which
is defined as ”electrical work” for the purposes of the
Licensing Of
Electrical Contractors And Master Electricians
Regulation.
T
herefore, the prosecution has proven beyond a
reasonable doubt that defendant has committed the offence of “operating an
electrical contracting business without holding a valid electrical contractor
licence” in respect to 22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton, between April 1, 2014
to July 22, 2014, contrary to s. 3 of the
Licensing Of Electrical
Contractors And Master Electricians
Regulation (
Electricity Act, 1998
),

O. Reg. 570/05
.

[475]

In respect to count #2, the defendant, who was not a licensed
electrician or a licenced electrical contractor in Ontario, had informed Ahmed
Khan, the homeowner of 291 Boon Avenue, Toronto that he was an electrician.
Ahmed Khan had hired the defendant by a written agreement to renovate his
house.  The defendant had worked on the renovation of Khan’s house from March
24, 2013, when the agreement had been signed, to about of the end of December
of 2013, when the defendant stopping doing any work on Khan’s house.  Although
the written agreement did not specifically mention that the defendant had to do
any electrical work, except for removing electrical in the demolition work,
Khan had observed the defendant doing electrical work in his basement while the
defendant had been standing in a pool of water on the basement floor, which
included running wire through the joists from the electrical panel, which had
caused Khan to be concerned for the defendant’s safety as well as for Khan’s
safety since the defendant was doing electrical work while standing in water.  Khan
also said he had observed the defendant put electrical outlets in the studs
before the drywall was put up.  In addition, when the defendant fell behind in
the renovation, Khan authorized the defendant to bring in Steve Duff to help the
defendant do the electrical work.  Khan also had observed the defendant and
Steve Duff  work together doing electrical work in the house at 291 Boon Avenue
for about a week and a half in December of 2013.  Khan had also testified to
having observed the defendant running and pulling wire in the basement, which
is defined as ”electrical work” for the purposes of the
Licensing Of
Electrical Contractors And Master Electricians
Regulation.
T
herefore, the prosecution has proven beyond a
reasonable doubt that defendant has committed the offence of “operating an
electrical contracting business without holding a valid electrical contractor
licence” in respect to 291 Boon Avenue, Toronto, from December 2, 2013 to April
30, 2014, contrary to s. 3 of the
Licensing Of Electrical Contractors And
Master Electricians
Regulation (
Electricity Act, 1998
),
O. Reg.
570/05
.

[476]

In respect to count #3, the defendant, had been hired by the
homeowner Razeka Bacchus to repair and renovate the main floor of her house
after it had been damaged and vandalized in a break-in.  The defendant had
worked on the renovation of Bacchus’s house from August 8,  2011, to December
31, 2012.  Razeka Bacchus did not testify that the renovation work included the
defendant doing electrical work.  Bacchus only testified that the defendant was
supposed to put in 16 pot lights with switches and that if the defendant did
not know how to do something that it was expected that he would bring in
someone properly licenced that would know how to do it.  Moreover, Bacchus did
not see the defendant do any electrical work in her house and only saw a young
man drilling holes for the pot lights.  Therefore, the prosecution has failed
to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that
the defendant

has committed the offence of “operating an electrical contracting
business without holding a valid electrical contractor licence” in respect to
94 Narrow Valley Crescent, Brampton, from August 8,  2011 to December 31, 2012,
contrary to s. 3 of the
Licensing Of Electrical Contractors And Master
Electricians
Regulation (
Electricity Act, 1998
),
O. Reg. 570/05
.

7.            DISPOSITION

[477]

Ergo, in respect to count #1, based on the totality of the
evidence, the prosecution has fulfilled its burden in proving in proving beyond
a reasonable doubt that Paul Broomfield had, in regards to
Jay Jairam’s house at 22 Vespahills Crescent, Brampton,
committed
the offence of “operating an electrical contracting business without holding a
valid electrical contractor licence” from April 1, 2014 to July 22, 2014,
contrary to s. 3 of the
Licensing Of Electrical Contractors And Master
Electricians
Regulation (
Electricity Act, 1998
),
O. Reg. 570/05
, and
therefore committed an offence under
s. 113.20(1)
(d) of the
Electricity
Act, 1998
, S.O. 1998, c. 15, Sched. A.  Therefore,
a conviction
will be entered against Paul Broomfield
in respect to count #1.

[478]

And, in respect to count #2,
based
on the totality of the evidence, the prosecution has fulfilled its burden in
proving beyond a reasonable doubt that Paul Broomfield had, in regards to
Ahmed Khan’s house at 291 Boon Avenue, Toronto,
committed
the offence of “operating an electrical contracting business without holding a
valid electrical contractor licence” from December 2, 2013 to April 30, 2014,
contrary to s. 3 of the
Licensing Of Electrical Contractors And Master
Electricians
Regulation (
Electricity Act, 1998
),
O. Reg. 570/05
, and
therefore committed an offence under
s. 113.20(1)
(d) of the
Electricity
Act, 1998
, S.O. 1998, c. 15, Sched. A.  Therefore,
a conviction
will be entered against Paul Broomfield
in respect to count #2
.

[479]

And, in respect to count #3, the prosecution has
not
met
its burden in proving beyond a reasonable doubt that Paul Broomfield had, in
regards to
Razeka Bacchus’s house at 94 Narrow Valley
Crescent, Brampton,
committed the offence of “operating an electrical
contracting business without holding a valid electrical contractor licence” from
August 8,  2011 to December 31, 2012, contrary to s. 3 of the
Licensing Of
Electrical Contractors And Master Electricians
Regulation (
Electricity
Act, 1998
),
O. Reg. 570/05
.  Therefore,
an acquittal will be entered for
Paul Broomfield
in respect to count #3
.
